transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-30 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~75m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Product), Jordan Lee (CortexAI SRE), Maya Ruiz (CortexAI ML Eng), Evan Brooks (CortexAI Platform)

Summary (auto): Align on benchmark methodology and get concrete next steps for apples-to-apples microbenchmarks and production-like load tests.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through a practical workshop on methodology, not just numbers but how you get apples-to-apples. Quick intros?
[00:18] Jordan Lee: Jordan here, SRE at CortexAI, I own the serving infra and we want to validate performance on dedicated and private stacks.
[00:26] Maya Ruiz: Maya, ML Eng, mostly prompt sets and evals, we've been running ad-hoc tests but results vary a lot.
[00:32] Evan Brooks: Evan - platform lead, concerned about VPC throughputs and firewall/bandwidth constraints for on-prem.
[00:38] Alex Chen: Great. Priya, want to quick frame the agenda?
[00:41] Priya Nair: Yeah - we'll cover canonical prompt sets, how to capture production traces, load-gen tools and configs, warm vs cold KV cache behavior, batching strategies incl continuous batching, quantization differences (8-bit vs 4-bit), and network/VPC specifics for on-prem. Then we'll map to an experiment plan.
[01:05] Samir Patel: One ask from our side - we want clear metrics to compare: per-token p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and kernel-level memory footprints.
[01:18] Priya Nair: Agreed — also measure cold vs warm latencies and cache hit rates; KV cache significantly changes tail latency because of prefix reuse.
[01:31] Jordan Lee: Quick Q - when you say apples-to-apples, how do you control for model variants (fp16 vs quantized) and different runtime kernels?
[01:40] Priya Nair: Good point. We recommend defining a matrix: model architecture + weight precision (fp16, 8-bit, 4-bit) + kernel/runtime flags. For apples-to-apples, keep payloads, prompt sets and sequence distribution identical, and log exact model artifact sha and quant profile.
[02:01] Maya Ruiz: We're worried about quantization artifacts on quality for some prompts. Any suggestions for evaluation?
[02:08] Alex Chen: Use a small eval set of critical prompts from prod and automated metrics (perplexity/embedding cosine on reference outputs) plus human spot checks. Keep the eval set consistent across runs.
[02:22] Jordan Lee: On load generation - we use Locust internally, but our traces are more bursty than synthetic fixed-rps. Thoughts?
[02:31] Priya Nair: We generally do two parallel approaches: 1) Synthetic steady-state (wrk/hey/locust) to get throughput curves and 2) Replay of anonymized production traces to capture bursts and inter-arrival correlations which affect KV cache warming and batching efficiency.
[02:52] Evan Brooks: For production traces, what fields do you need? We can't share PII.
[02:57] Priya Nair: Anonymized timestamped requests, sequence lengths, prompt ids, client routing metadata. Remove PII but keep timing and token-length distribution. That helps emulate real concurrency and cache warmup.
[03:15] Samir Patel: Let's talk KV cache specifics - what warm strategies do you recommend for benchmarks?
[03:20] Priya Nair: Two modes: cold-start (no KV warm) and warmed prefix mode (preload common prefixes). Measure hit rate, average prefix reuse length, and p99 both warm and cold. Document the preload script and the exact prefixes used.
[03:36] Jordan Lee: How do you preload in Dedicated or Private? Does Redwood provide tooling?
[03:40] Alex Chen: We can provide a preload script in the benchmark harness; it uses batched requests to populate KV quickly. On private, it runs inside the VPC to avoid egress. We'll share an example.
[03:52] Maya Ruiz: For batching - there are multiple knobs: batch size, max wait, continuous batching vs manual. What do you typically recommend?
[03:58] Priya Nair: Continuous batching with adaptive max latency cap is common in production; for benchmarking you should sweep batch_size and max_delay (e.g., 8/32/128 and 5ms/20ms/100ms) and report both latency SLO breaches and tokens/sec. Also test per-client fairness.
[04:20] Jordan Lee: Is there a standard for sequence length distributions? Our workloads vary 8-2048 tokens.
[04:25] Priya Nair: Capture empirical distribution and run stratified tests: short (<64), medium (64-512), long (512+). Kit the workloads so you can aggregate weighted metrics matching real traffic.
[04:38] Alex Chen: Quantization - let's discuss pragmatic expectations. 8-bit quant (GPTQ/QLoRA-ish) can be near fp16 on many prompts, 4-bit often trades off with some quality depending on model. Also kernel selection and fused attention matter; some runtimes optimize 4-bit better than others.
[04:58] Samir Patel: We saw memory reductions but p99 got worse in a handful of prompts with 4-bit. Could that be kernel selection?
[05:05] Priya Nair: Could be—also attention kernel numerics. Log exact kernel versions and lib versions (cuBLAS/cuDNN/oneAPI equivalents). We record per-kernel op times if possible.
[05:21] Jordan Lee: For VPC/on-prem, the network becomes a constraint. What should we watch for?
[05:26] Alex Chen: Watch request/response sizes and egress bandwidth. If model tokens per request are large, you saturate network faster than GPU. Also TLS termination and proxying can add latency. We recommend running the inference component internal to the VPC and collect NIC metrics (p99, drops, retransmits).
[05:44] Maya Ruiz: Do you have benchmark examples for H100 vs A100 differences?
[05:48] Priya Nair: We keep a catalog but for apples-to-apples test the same kernel stacks and compare using normalized metrics like tokens/sec per GPU and cost per token. Raw GHz/RAM differences also show in sequence length ceilings.
[06:05] Evan Brooks: Security/compliance: we need SOC2 docs, KMS integration notes, and audit logs for Private.
[06:12] Alex Chen: We'll attach the security packet and KMS integrations. Private deployment supports external HSM/KMS and audit logs; we'll share the specifics.
[06:20] Jordan Lee: Walk through an example bench plan?
[06:23] Priya Nair: Sure - example plan: 1) Define prompt set (N=500 canonical prompts, stratified). 2) Collect sequence length distribution from prod traces. 3) Run cold-start single-request latencies on fp16, 8-bit, 4-bit. 4) Run steady-state throughput sweeps (rps increase) with warm KV preload. 5) Replay trace and measure p50/p95/p99 and cache hit rate. 6) Repeat on Dedicated and Private. Document every artifact.
[06:56] Maya Ruiz: For the canonical prompt set, should we include adversarial edge prompts?
[07:00] Priya Nair: Include edge cases that your product depends on—particularly long context and multi-turn prompts. Also include a quality eval subset.
[07:11] Jordan Lee: On measurement tools: you mentioned collecting kernel timings. How intrusive is that?
[07:17] Priya Nair: We ship optional low-overhead hooks in the runtime; otherwise you can enable extra tracing that adds small overhead. For strict apples-to-apples, apply the same tracing flags across runs and note the measurement overhead.
[07:31] Samir Patel: Regarding load generators - any gotchas when using locust vs wrk?
[07:36] Priya Nair: Locust is good for high-level behavioral tests with user scenarios, wrk/hey/wrk2 for raw throughput. Ensure client-side batching or connection reuse isn't masking server behavior; e.g., HTTP keepalive matters.
[07:51] Jordan Lee: What about autoscaling behavior and its interaction with benchmarks?
[07:54] Alex Chen: For Dedicated tests, turn autoscaling off for baseline runs, then test autoscale-incurred jitter separately. Autoscaling can mask steady-state performance but reflects production economics.
[08:06] Maya Ruiz: Cold-start vs warm starts - we saw big gaps in p99. How to report both?
[08:10] Priya Nair: Report both explicitly and include transition curves (latency over time) during trace replay. Also report cache hit rate and KV entries size.
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Any recommended logs to capture for debugging regressions?
[08:23] Priya Nair: Per-request trace id, model sha, quant profile, kernel version, batch size, cache hit flag, and end-to-end timing broken down (recv->queue->compute->serialize).
[08:39] Samir Patel: For apples-to-apples cost comparisons, should we include amortized infra and license costs per token?
[08:45] Alex Chen: Yes — tokens per second and cost per 1M tokens is a good normalized metric. Also include tail-latency penalties separately since user experience is not linear with cost.
[08:59] Jordan Lee: When comparing hosted vs private, how to control for network differences?
[09:03] Priya Nair: Try to colocate load generator in same region/VPC or run internal load generator in customer's VPC to avoid internet egress effects. If not possible, measure network RTT and subtract network time from end-to-end to isolate runtime latency.
[09:20] Maya Ruiz: On batching - is there a standard way to simulate adaptive batching at client-side?
[09:25] Priya Nair: Use a replay driver that replays requests at timestamps and avoids artificial client-side batching unless that's part of the product. For adaptive batching tests, simulate many clients with varied inter-arrival times and let the runtime batch naturally.
[09:42] Alex Chen: Let's get concrete - we'll post a benchmark harness repo with examples: preload scripts, locust + wrk configs, a canonical prompt set, and a results ingestion spreadsheet.
[09:51] Jordan Lee: Good. One more: metrics during GC or memory pressure - do you recommend long-run stability tests?
[09:57] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Run soak tests (6-24 hours) to catch memory leaks or degradation, and record throughput over time.
[10:09] Maya Ruiz: For quantization, can you share the config file you use when you do 4-bit runs?
[10:13] Alex Chen: We'll share quant profiles and the exact quantization toolchain versions. Document the random seeds and any per-layer clamps.
[10:24] Jordan Lee: Will Redwood run these POCs in our VPC or do we need to provide infra?
[10:29] Alex Chen: We have two options: 1) we run the harness inside your VPC with a lightweight agent, or 2) we provide dedicated infra in our account and you run remote repros. For apples-to-apples with network isolation, option 1 is preferred.
[10:45] Evan Brooks: Network egress and firewall will need a pre-approved egress rule; we'll coordinate.
[10:49] Alex Chen: Noted. We'll give the exact CIDR and ports for the preload and monitoring endpoints.
[10:55] Priya Nair: Let's talk p99 and tail - if you have long-tail outliers, often it's due to cache misses or GC pauses. Correlate p99 spikes with cache hit flags and host metrics.
[11:09] Jordan Lee: On host metrics, do you have recommended thresholds for GPU utilization vs latency tradeoff?
[11:14] Priya Nair: There's no single threshold. But report GPU util vs tokens/sec and latency; high util with increasing p99 suggests you're saturating compute. If p99 rises with low util, it's often external (network, GC).
[11:29] Samir Patel: For private on-prem we might be on older drivers. How much impact should we expect?
[11:34] Priya Nair: Driver and CUDA/cuDNN versions can impact kernel performance notably. Record exact driver/library versions and ideally run the same microbench kernel tests across environments to isolate performance deltas.
[11:48] Maya Ruiz: Are there non-obvious measurement pitfalls you've seen?
[11:52] Priya Nair: Yes - client-side fanouts, hidden proxies, TLS offload, or logging at high verbosity can skew latency. Also clock skew between machines affects time series; use monotonic timers or synchronized clocks.
[12:09] Jordan Lee: For KV cache size and eviction - how do you choose eviction policy during bench?
[12:15] Priya Nair: Document policy (LRU, TTL), entry sizes, and eviction thresholds. For reproducibility, start with a clean cache and document the exact size limits.
[12:28] Alex Chen: Let's show an example result shape: you'll have matrices across precision/kernel/batch where each cell has tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99, cache hit rate, GPU util and cost per token.
[12:44] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Can we get a sample spreadsheet?
[12:47] Alex Chen: Yes — will send after the call.
[12:50] Priya Nair: Any concerns about multi-tenant noise for hosted?
[12:54] Jordan Lee: We prefer dedicated for POC to avoid noise.
[12:57] Alex Chen: Recommended — Dedicated or Private for deterministic baselines.
[13:03] Maya Ruiz: On measuring end-to-end experience, should we also simulate downstream app latency?
[13:07] Priya Nair: Good idea — capture full app stack time to ensure no unexpected bottlenecks outside inference.
[13:17] Evan Brooks: Regarding SSO and audit logs - can you confirm log retention options for Private?
[13:22] Alex Chen: Yes, retention is configurable; we'll share the options and costs.
[13:29] Jordan Lee: One more Q - for apples-to-apples, do you pin GPU clock/boost states?
[13:34] Priya Nair: If possible, pin performance states and document them. Variance in power management causes jitter.
[13:44] Maya Ruiz: For ephemeral batch noise, how many runs do you average?
[13:48] Priya Nair: Usually 5 runs per config and report median plus interquartile ranges; for p99 use bootstrap confidence intervals.
[13:58] Samir Patel: Anything else on quantization tests?
[14:01] Priya Nair: Check out-of-vocab tokens and sampling variance; use fixed seeds for deterministic decoding during bench.
[14:11] Jordan Lee: Ok I think we have enough to start. We'll pull prod traces and share.
[14:15] Alex Chen: Great. Quick recap of action items and next steps?
[14:19] Priya Nair: Recap - Alex sends spreadsheet and prompt set; Priya prepares Dedicated config + harness; CortexAI provides traces and prompt list; we target small POC in us-west-2; follow-up week of 2026-04-13.
[14:36] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, that works.
[14:39] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links and the security packet.

End of transcript.
